implementation_notes: The current pact-python interface is a thin layer over the Rust core: Pact('user-consumer', 'user-provider').with_specification('V4') names the contract, the fluent upon_receiving/given/with_request/will_respond_with/with_body chain declares one interaction, match.int()/match.str()/match.datetime() keep response fields loose, and `with pact.serve() as srv:` starts the mock service whose URL replaces the provider's base URL in the client under test; pact.write_file(dir) emits the contract when the pytest fixture tears down. The earlier generation of the same library instead drove the pact-ruby-standalone CLI (spec v2, pending/WIP pact support), which is why the two generations are worth distinguishing.
code_sketch:
@pytest.fixture
def pact():
    p = Pact("user-consumer", "user-provider").with_specification("V4")
    yield p
    p.write_file("pacts")                 # contract emitted after the test

def test_get_user(pact):
    (pact.upon_receiving("A user request").given("the user exists", id=123)
         .with_request("GET", "/users/123").will_respond_with(200)
         .with_body({"id": match.int(123), "name": match.str("Alice")},
                    content_type="application/json"))
    with pact.serve() as srv:
        assert UserClient(str(srv.url)).get_user(123).name == "Alice"
pitfalls: Calling the mock service with a generic HTTP client (requests, httpx) instead of the client under test verifies nothing - the request assertions are the point of the test.
Every declared interaction must be exercised: an unused one fails the test when the pact.serve() block exits, which is where a forgotten call surfaces.
The matching core ships as a native FFI library, so platforms without a compatible wheel cannot run the suite; keep it in a test-only dependency group so it never reaches production.

variants.name: pact-python v2 driving the pact-ruby-standalone CLI (spec V2)
variants.idiom_name: older pact-python API served by the pact-ruby-standalone mock service
variants.implementation_notes: The first pact-python generation shells out to the pact-ruby-standalone CLI: the consumer test builds its interactions through the older Python API while a Ruby mock service process serves them, and contracts are written as spec v2 (that generation verifies v3 files but honours only the v2 matching rules). It remains a fallback for projects pinned to the older API or to environments where the native core cannot be loaded, but new work should use the FFI interface, which speaks V3/V4 and keeps the mock service in-process.
pitfalls: The mock service is an external Ruby process: a crashed or unreachable service turns into connection errors that look like client bugs, and CI images must carry the standalone CLI.

Contracts produced by this generation are spec v2, so V4 features (plugins, synchronous messages, cross-field matchers) are unavailable, and mixing generations in one repository yields inconsistent files.
